touches.text: Owns the CC launcher (superclaude): starts Claude Code with Cairn's session contract, in its own memory-capped cgroup. WHY: Claude can OOM the box.

superclaude is Python on every box, launched by the platform shell (5.4.3.8.5), and inherits the elevation the shell settled (5.4.3.8.6): elevated PowerShell on Windows, sudo with IS_SANDBOX=1 on Linux; it never elevates itself. - akiendelllinux_orchestrator

Scripts are Python wherever possible, run by Cairn's own interpreter, so one file works on every platform. Platform-specific ones match their platform: executable or .sh on Linux; .bat, .cmd or .ps1 on Windows.
The launcher is Python (bin/cairn), run by Cairn's own interpreter, so Windows needs no bash. Typing `cairn` works on either platform.

Each platform shell does two things, in order, before handing over: it elevates, then it runs Cairn's own Python on the launcher (on Windows `@python <path>\cairn ...`; on Linux the same without the @). Every decision after that is Python's; the shell holds no other logic beyond the fall-over above.

Elevation is the shell's, settled before Python starts, and nothing inside asks again. On Windows the shell runs in an elevated PowerShell. On Linux the shell sudoes the launch, with IS_SANDBOX=1 set so Claude Code accepts bypass permissions under root. WHY: the whole box is the sandbox, so elevating once at launch is simpler than elevating on request; IS_SANDBOX=1 is set on every box for that reason. - akiendelllinux_orchestrator
Code that is no longer needed is deleted. Git history keeps it if we ever need it back.

Deleting code is about running code, not about the record of what happened. A retired path that something still CALLS is the defect; a retired path named by a record of what passed through (history, state, validations, verdicts, a measured fixture) is not. Requirements that police history are de-emphasized, because the aim is less history noise in front of Claude, not hidden history (Law 5).

A retirement checks its callers in the same act as the deletion: nothing imports the module being deleted, and nothing runs the command or path being deleted. A file that only names it (a fixture, a record, a charter) is not a caller. Nothing checks afterwards. Why? Naming is history; only a caller breaks, and a caller that comes later breaks loudly on its own. A standing proof that a thing stays gone is history kept as code.

`cairn codemother retire <path>...` does the deletion. It runs the proofs of the files that name the target, before and after moving it aside. A proof that turns red is a caller, and the target goes back. Why? Running a proof tells a caller from a mention; reading the text cannot.
tester
INTENTION:
Test runs are transient (30 days, 4.3.2); seals are records of truth (git).

Commit: the proofs of the component the ticket changed, since RULE 1 bounds a change to its component. Passing them puts the component in service, yellow: proven where it changed, not yet measured against what depends on it. In service needs only the best we can do now: 80% trust.

A rule not yet enforced is made into a ticket now, never left floating as prose. So ticket f5dbfddea8c6 makes the rewrites it proposed at the remaining sites (the press office, PROOF.md). Where a site names a rule whose physics is not built, it names that rule's real ticket id, cast now if none exists; the word "ticket" with no id behind it does not count. - CC
build_inspector

The inspectors are not assumed correct; they are examined when they refuse. After a gate refuses, an LLM sets the refusing sieve's intention and why beside the ticket's intention and why and asks: is this sieve the best we can do right now? If yes, the ticket changes. If no, the sieve is fixed through its own ticket and proof. Either way the system improves. WHY: a disagreement becomes an update to an intention or its implementation, never a conversation about procedure. The sieves stay deterministic and never weigh a why; the LLM check comes only after a failure, and it is never a lock pick because it has no third outcome. Nothing passes a ticket over a red.

Any device or machine may have a bin/ beside its code. That folder IS its list of shortcuts: add a file to add one, delete it to remove one. A shortcut is a script that calls the long form (eg `cairn superclaude` -> `cairn cc superclaude`; `cairn show temp` -> `cairn recovery show temp`), which also saves the walk from searching farther, or does work itself (eg install). Shortcuts live beside what they serve (RULE 1). `cairn foo` whose first word is not a device means `cairn cairn foo`: top-level shortcuts are the cairn device's bin/.
Any cairn command brings up whatever it needs, including the whole install on the very first run (6.3.2). WHY: a well designed tool should disappear in use.

Every device has a shim. Each shim is its own process, one per instance, and connects to the bus as a client. WHY: in the bus process, updating one shim meant bringing the whole bus down, and one shim's stall was everyone's. Separate, a shim restarts itself when its own files change, like the ground loop, and the bus stays up.
pulse.py is part of the shim. The ground loop calling it tells the shim the pulse has arrived, and starts the shim if it isn't running.

The ground loop finds one pulse.py per device. pulse.py reads its own device's declared instances (5.7.3.4) and pulses each one, so the ground loop never needs to know instances exist. Pulsing an instance that isn't connected is what starts its shim.

pulse.py asks nobody anything. It starts the shim if it's down, else tells the mechanisms inside the shim that need a pulse "here ya go!" Only daemon-shaped things hang there, things that actually need a heartbeat (eg cc's Gmail fetch, 10.3.6); everything else fires on events. WHY: pulse.py is a place to hang daemons from, not managers.

The abstract ticket owns what every kind shares: its birth (cast) and its three parts, each with one job: the plan (only what a builder builds from), the metadata and state (what gates and doors read and write as it moves), and the history (the append-only log). WHY: one job per part reduces confusion; a builder reads the plan and nothing else.
Commit often. WHY: so we never wind up with stray files or incomplete work.
Coding Ticket: what we usually mean.
The very first run:

Install and upgrades live here: the installer machine walks the host-seam intentions, verifies each, offers what's missing, applies, re-verifies. If xyz library needs an update, this is the component that does it. Any change to what the host is goes through here (6.6.3.1.1).
A command goes in, runs as root, and a permanent audit record comes out: the command line, return code, stdout, stderr, plus an id and date. The audit folder keeps a rolling one month.
rehearsal: the cheapest model reads a ticket cold and tries to build it on paper, saying where it got stopped or what is missing.

WHY: a simulation costs tokens; it earns them only by teaching a tree. It was never meant to catch every shortcoming of every ticket, and where it teaches nothing it costs more than the builder simply building and recording where it got stuck. So until a learner reads the records, a rehearsal is not a BUILDME requirement; the records stand as the learner's first corpus.
base device: the base class for every internal device.

artifact: the one door a record of truth changes through, and the journal of who came through it (hash-chained, caller read from the kernel). WHY: errors are permanent in records of truth (Law 7), and the journal is what shows a record moved by hand. USERS: everyone who writes a record.
import_sieve: one parse of every .py into an import graph; what reaches what. WHY: enforces "only the proxy reaches the host/database" and RULE 1 by physics. USERS: CodeMother, the inference proxy.
A new shortcut needs no watch. Most instance bins are links to their class bin, so the shortcut is reachable the moment its file lands; the build's proof is the whole guarantee.

In front of it sits a thin platform shell (a shell script on Linux, cairn.cmd or cairn.ps1 on Windows) with enough brains to fall over to Rescue (6.5) when it can't find Cairn's Python, or Python throws, or anything else stops the launcher. The failure throws a trouble ticket (3.4.3), and the ticket is Rescue's "read this" (6.5.3.5); a repeat increments that ticket's counter. Rescue's prompt says: at the end of proving the fix, check for more errors, to clear or fix as appropriate. WHY: trouble has to be able to report when nothing else can (2.3.7.1.3).
